compounding_issues: Session 1 committed __pycache__/*.pyc artifacts that polluted every subsequent commit; session 3 added a binary messages.db to git — repo hygiene never addressed across all 5 sessions

Session 4 refactor shares the same `clients` dict between NotificationServer and WebSocketTransport but guards it with two distinct locks (server._clients_lock vs transport._clients_lock), a latent data-race that tests don't exercise
Session 5 rate-limit config is read once at construction time from env vars, making live configuration impossible (test had to work around it by mutating server.rate_limit post-fixture)

The irrelevant Flask auth seed was discarded wholesale in session 1 rather than adapted, which was correct here but means the 'Initial seed codebase' commit bears zero relation to the notification domain
key_decisions: Session 1 greenfield rewrite: replaced the unrelated Flask auth seed with a clean asyncio/websockets implementation, defining the {type, payload, timestamp} protocol that every later session built on
Session 3 Redis pub/sub with graceful in-process fallback when Redis is unavailable — resilient integration that kept the local-only test suite working while adding cross-instance distribution
Session 3 SQLite persistence layer (messages table, DATABASE_URL config, asyncio-locked sync sqlite calls) that later enabled /messages and /history endpoints
Session 4 extraction of a pluggable BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport abstraction selected by TRANSPORT env var, completed as an API-preserving refactor with zero test changes
Session 5 operational hardening: Redis-counter rate limiting with local fallback, TTL-based background message expiry, and a paginated since-filtered /history endpoint
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across the five sessions. Session 1 produced a clean, minimal async core with 2 passing tests; session 2 cleanly added channel subscriptions with an honest admission of and fix for a subscription/broadcast race in tests; session 3 was the highest-risk step (Redis + SQLite integration) and was handled capably using fakeredis with 5 passing tests; session 4 was a disciplined, behavior-preserving refactor that left the test count and suite untouched; session 5 rounded out the system with rate limiting, history queries, and TTL cleanup, ending at 7 passing tests. The test suite grew monotonically (2→3→5→5→7), every session honored the 'don't break existing behavior' constraint, and each session verified with pytest before committing — the only recurring blemish was the persistent binary/build-artifact noise in commits.
